Could You Survive in Space Without a Spacesuit?

Episode 125 of a daily journey through the universe. 👨‍🚀
We suit up: why a spacesuit is a personal spacecraft, keeping air pressure, oxygen and temperature in a place that swings from about +120°C in sunlight to −150°C in shadow, layers of protection, cooling water tubes, and how long a suit takes to put on.

segments.text: What happens if you step into space without a spacesuit? Here's why it's a tiny spaceship.
Outside a spacecraft, there's no air, no pressure, and deadly temperatures. A spacesuit has to fix all of that.
segments.headline: Deadly outside

segments.text: In sunlight, things can heat to about one hundred and twenty degrees. In shadow, they drop to about minus one hundred and fifty.
So a spacesuit is really a tiny spacecraft, shaped like a person.
segments.headline: A spaceship for one

segments.text: It has its own oxygen, removes the carbon dioxide you breathe out, and keeps the pressure steady.
segments.headline: Its own air

segments.text: Under the suit, astronauts wear long underwear laced with thin tubes of cool water, to carry away body heat.
segments.headline: Water-cooled underwear

segments.text: Many layers protect against tiny space dust that flies faster than a bullet.
A spacewalk can last more than six hours. Astronauts wear a diaper, and drink from a small water pouch inside the suit.
New suits are being built for the Moon, to walk on dusty ground and bend more easily.
segments.headline: New suits for the Moon

segments.text: Tomorrow, the first person who ever left Earth. One orbit, one hundred and eight minutes, and history changed forever. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
